title: Reinforcing and Balancing Behavior Lab
creator: Dan McCreary
subject: MicroSims
System Dynamics
Feedback Loops
Reinforcing Loop
Balancing Loop
Predict-Observe-Explain
description: A p5.js MicroSim that plots a reinforcing loop (x = x + rate*x) and a balancing loop (x = x + rate*(goal - x)) side by side so learners can compare exponential growth with goal-seeking behavior, with an optional prediction step after each slider change.
audience: Teachers, instructional designers, learning-technology developers and learning-analytics practitioners (college undergraduate and professional development)

educational.topic: Time behavior of reinforcing and balancing feedback loops
learningObjectives: The learner will compare the time behavior of a reinforcing loop and a balancing loop by changing the loop rate and the goal and observing the resulting curves.
prerequisites: Feedback loop, polarity link, reinforcing loop and balancing loop (Chapter 8)
Reading a line graph over time

accessibility.notes: describe() summary for screen readers; curves use shape (circles vs squares) and letters (R, B) as well as color; all controls are native HTML buttons, sliders and a checkbox

controls.label: Start / Pause
controls.purpose: Run or pause the 50-step simulation (starts paused)

controls.label: Reset
controls.purpose: Return both curves to the start value and clear the prediction state

controls.label: Predict first
controls.purpose: Pause after each slider change and ask whether each curve will rise faster, slower or the same

controls.label: Faster / Slower / Same (R and B)
controls.purpose: Record a prediction for each curve (shown only while a prediction is pending)

pedagogical.interactionPattern: Parameter sliders with a prediction gate and a ghost of the previous run
keyQuestions: Why does the reinforcing curve bend upward while the balancing curve bends toward the goal?
Why does raising the goal change only the balancing curve?
Why does a higher start value speed up R but slow down B?
commonMisconceptions: A balancing loop always keeps a value low (it moves the value toward a goal, which can mean rising)
Both loops respond the same way to a higher start value (R responds to the value, B to the gap)
assessmentOpportunities: First-try accuracy of the R and B predictions
Written comparison of the two update rules

assumptions: One loop acts alone on each curve, with no delays or limits
Both curves share the same rate and start value
limitations: Real learner systems combine several loops and delays
Units are abstract stock units and time steps
